**Janissaries and the devshirme**
The Janissaries were the elite infantry corps that guarded the sultan and formed the core of the Ottoman army. They were recruited through the devshirme ("collection," sometimes called the "blood tax"), in which Christian boys, mostly from the Balkans, were taken from their families, converted to Islam, and trained for military or civil service.

**Suleiman the Magnificent**
The sultan who ruled from 1520 to 1566, under whom the empire reached its peak. Known in Turkish as "the Lawgiver" (Kanuni) for his legal codes blending sultanic law with sharia, he won at Mohács, took Belgrade, Rhodes, and Baghdad, besieged Vienna in 1529, and married Roxelana (Hürrem Sultan).

**Mehmed II and the fall of Constantinople (1453)**
Mehmed II, "the Conqueror," captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire. He made the city (later Istanbul) his capital and converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque, adding minarets to the former Orthodox cathedral.

**Auspicious Incident (1826)**
Sultan Mahmud II's forcible destruction of the Janissary corps after they revolted against his military reforms. Thousands of Janissaries were killed, many executed in Thessaloniki's "Blood Tower," clearing the way for a modern, European-style army.

**Tanzimat and the Edict of Gülhane**
The Tanzimat ("reorganization") was a period of Westernizing, centralizing reforms from 1839 to 1876. It began with the 1839 Edict of Gülhane (the "Noble Edict of the Rose Chamber"), which guaranteed subjects' lives and property, abolished tax farming, and reformed taxation and conscription; later reforms reorganized the millet system.

**Sieges of Vienna (1529 and 1683)**
Suleiman's 1529 siege of Vienna marked the limit of Ottoman expansion into Central Europe. The 1683 siege under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa was broken at the Battle of Kahlenberg by the Holy League led by Polish king Jan III Sobieski, whose Winged Hussars made one of history's largest cavalry charges; legends say the croissant (kipferl) and Vienna's coffeehouses came from this victory.

**Battle of Mohács (1526)**
Suleiman's crushing victory over King Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia, who died fleeing the battle. It ended the Jagiellonian line in Hungary and led to Hungary being partitioned between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs.

**"Sick Man of Europe"**
A nickname for the declining Ottoman Empire in the 19th and early 20th centuries, tied to the "Eastern Question" of what would happen to its territories. The empire joined the Central Powers in World War I, defended Gallipoli against the Allies, and was dissolved after the war.

**Battle of Lepanto (1571)**
A naval battle in which the Holy League fleet, commanded by Don John of Austria, destroyed much of the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras. It checked Ottoman naval power in the Mediterranean, though the fleet was quickly rebuilt.

**Hayreddin Barbarossa**
The Ottoman admiral and corsair who commanded Suleiman's navy. In an alliance with Francis I of France, he helped the French besiege Nice in 1543.

**Topkapi Palace, the harem, and the valide sultan**
Topkapi in Istanbul was the sultans' palace and seat of government. Its imperial harem was overseen by the Chief Black Eunuch, and the valide sultan (the sultan's mother) held great power, especially during the "Sultanate of Women" that began around Suleiman's marriage to Roxelana and lasted about a century.

**Fratricide and the kafes**
To prevent succession wars, new sultans often had their brothers killed; Mehmed III had his 19 brothers strangled with silk cords in 1595. This was later replaced by the kafes ("cage"), where princes were confined in the palace, which is blamed for rulers like Ibrahim "the Mad."

**Osman I and his dream**
Osman I founded the dynasty and gave the empire its name in Anatolia around 1300. Legend says he dreamt of a giant tree growing from his navel and spreading over the world, foretelling the empire. New sultans were girded with the Sword of Osman at their accession.

**Young Turks and the Committee of Union and Progress**
The reformist Young Turk movement, organized as the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), took power after 1908 and dominated the government during the Balkan Wars and World War I. It carried out genocides of Armenians, Assyrians (the Sayfo), and Greeks.

**Treaty of Karlowitz (1699)**
The treaty ending the Great Turkish War that followed the failed 1683 siege of Vienna. The Ottomans gave up most of Hungary to the Habsburgs and the Morea (Peloponnese) to Venice, the first major loss of territory in Europe.

**Treaty of Sèvres and the end of the empire**
The 1920 treaty that carved up the empire after World War I. It was rejected by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's nationalists, who won the Turkish War of Independence, abolished the sultanate in 1922 (ending the reign of the last sultan, Mehmed VI), and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923.
